name: Luriquay

facts.text: Level 65, 10,000 health, in the Cursed Forest; when he dies a Flame (level 64) rises from him.
Bot chat: he haunts the cursed forest and has ended more groups than the werewolves.

In Cath Maige Tuired, Lugh comes to Nuada's feast at Tara; the doorkeeper turns away each art he names, until Lugh asks whether the king has one man with all of them, and he is admitted and seated in the sage's seat.

story:
The lurikeens are the small quick folk who helped the elves raise the Veil, the lurikeens' own tales say, and most of them went behind it. Luriquay did not. He stayed in the court wood, the Ardee folk say, because he liked the bargaining and the fires and the company, and when the bargain broke he drank from the hearth-fire to keep warm through the long bad night that followed. A spark of it stayed in him.

He looks like nothing much, a lurikeen gone wrong, which is how he has ended more bands than the werewolves of the forest. He is quick and hard and mocking, and when he falls the spark comes out, a new Flame as hungry as the old one, and the bands who cheer early learn the warm way. The lurikeens of Tir na Nog do not talk about him. When asked, they say he was always the clever one.

The lurikeen lore of Tir na Nog is silent about what they owe him. Some say he held the court wood's door for them the night they went behind the Veil.

When the lurikeens of Tir na Nog do speak of him, and are feeling kind, they compare him to Lugh at the door of Tara. When Nuada of the Silver Hand held his feast at Tara, the doorkeeper asked the young stranger at the gate what art he had, because no one came in without one. Lugh named his arts one after another, wright, smith, champion, harper, poet, sorcerer, physician, and each time the doorkeeper said the king already had a man for that. Then Lugh asked whether the king had one man who had all of them. The doorkeeper went in and asked, and Lugh was let in as the master of every art and sat in the sage's seat. The small folk like that story better than any other in the old tellings, because it is the one where the clever one wins by being asked the right question.

Luriquay was the clever one at the court wood's door, if the lurikeens' tale is true, and the night the bargain broke nobody asked him anything at all. Nobody has asked him anything since. Those who go into the Cursed Forest after him go with swords, not questions, and when he falls the fire comes out of him as if it had been waiting all those years to answer.
legend: He looks easy and is not: bring a proper group. When he dies a Flame rises from his body at once, so be ready for a second fight and keep your wards against heat up. The bands who cheer early are the ones the old hibs tell stories about. Proper group, not a pair. Be ready for the Flame that rises from his body. Superstition: never call a lurikeen small within earshot of the Cursed Forest. Nicknames: 'the clever one', 'little luri'. The lurikeens of Tir na Nog leave a cup of milk out the night he is killed, and will not say whether it is for him or against him.

loremasterTopic.text: A small quick one who stayed in the court wood and drank its fire. He carries a Flame inside him, and it comes out when he dies.

bookPage: Grandmother knew a lurikeen in Tir na Nog, an old one, and asked him once about Luriquay; it is the next thing on Derbáil of Ardee's list. He was quiet for a long time, which lurikeens never are. Then he said: when our people went behind the Veil, he stayed, because he liked the bargaining and the fires. He was always the clever one. He drank from the court hearth on the bad night, to keep warm, and it stayed in him. Grandmother asked if that made him wicked. The lurikeen said: it made him warm. Then he changed the subject. When she pressed him, he said only that the clever one had once held a door, and nobody had thanked him for it.
